items.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06
items.q: Jay Cave was a bass player from Philly who had played with Nita Simone, John Erdly, Benny Goodman.

ctx.x: Yeah. Well, he drove all the better drummers away because by that time I was into my English teaching career and he pissed them off so badly that they wouldn't work with him anymore.

But another thing he did. And this goes back to it's very important in New Orleans to have outside influences because what happens, like in the case of Maus, you get these outside influences, they come to the city, Bill Evans is another example, they develop. And they develop, it's a give and take, it's a compromise with the city. They absorb things from the city and the city absorbs things from them. And I think that connection is really important. Anyway, it's kind of New York in a way. It's kind of what's been…

items.title: Bill Huntington Interview, 1961-12-27
items.q: And then I began to listen to, to, uh, I guess Teddy Wilson and Coleman Hawkins and people of that sort. And Benny Goodman.

ctx.x: Sure. Yeah, just talk. Just say anything that comes to your mind. No, I'd rather not do that. . .

Well, uh, when I was about fifteen, uh, uh, actually through the efforts of Alvin Purnell. You see, I used to sit in with George Lewis and Alvin Purnell had a thing going where he'd play passing chords. And, uh, I was told when I was a kid that I had some kind of fantastic gear. I was some kind of child prodigy or something, you see. And so, uh, I'd hear all the things he was playing. And I'd tell Lawrence, why aren't you playing the same chords Alton's playing? You know, they sound like they're fitting more into…
Who did you like when you started playing? You mentioned Bonk, and then there must have been some other musicians. You said you met a lot on the mind.
